summary: Arabic has singular, dual and plural; sound plurals (-ūn/-īn, -āt) and broken plurals. Most vegetables are collective nouns: جَزَر (carrots, as a kind); one piece is the unit noun جَزَرَة, counted pieces take -āt: جَزَرَات.

askYourself: Do I mean the vegetable in general (→ collective) or counted pieces (→ unit noun, plural -āt)?

traps: The sound feminine plural has -i (not -a) in the accusative: الْجَزَرَاتِ.
Non-human plurals take feminine singular agreement.

notes.text: Greek plurals change the ending (βιβλίο → βιβλία); Arabic most often changes the inside of the word (كِتَاب → كُتُب), has a dual for two, and treats plurals of things as feminine singular.
Russian has unit nouns like the Arabic ones: горох → горошина (a pea), картофель → картофелина (a potato) — compare بَصَل → بَصَلَة (an onion). New are the dual and the broken plurals.
Spanish adds -s / -es to every noun; most Arabic plurals are broken — a new vowel pattern inside the word (قَلَم → أَقْلَام) — and are learned with each noun.
English has a few inside-the-word plurals (foot → feet, man → men); in Arabic that is the most common kind (رَجُل → رِجَال), and there is a dual for two.
Hindi plurals change the ending by gender (लड़का → लड़के, किताब → किताबें); Arabic often changes the inside of the word and has a dual.
Persian uses Arabic broken plurals for many Arabic loanwords (کتب, اخبار) besides its own -hā / -ān, and even the Arabic ending -āt (سبزیجات, vegetables); in Arabic these are the normal plurals.
Turkish has one plural ending, -ler / -lar, and drops it after numbers; Arabic has three kinds of plural plus a dual, learned with each noun.
Japanese nouns usually do not mark plural; Arabic must choose singular, dual or plural every time.
Finnish plurals are regular (-t, -i-); Arabic plurals are mostly broken and are learned with each noun.
Hungarian adds -k (könyvek); Arabic mostly changes the vowels inside the word (كُتُب).
Swahili makes the plural by changing the prefix (kitabu → vitabu), Arabic often by changing the vowels inside (كِتَاب → كُتُب) — in both, learn the pair.
Luganda changes the class prefix (ekitabo → ebitabo), Arabic often changes the inside of the word — in both, learn the pair.
Vietnamese marks plural only with words like các / những; Arabic marks it on the noun itself, with a dual for two.
Inuktitut also has singular, dual and plural: inuk, inuuk, inuit (one, two, several people) — like Arabic -āni for two; but Arabic plurals are often broken.
